description:
We're a motivated team from India tackling the Earth Analogs challenge, building a data-driven tool that ranks Earth sites (like Ladakh and Atacama) by their similarity to lunar and Martian base locations, aiming for a global top-5 finish.
We're looking for teammates skilled in Python/data analysis, GIS or remote sensing, web/map visualization, and presentation or storytelling; join us if you want to work with real NASA data and help shape future Moon-to-Mars missions!
summary: TerraTwin is an analog portfolio planner that identifies and characterizes Earth locations for testing future Moon and Mars bases. No single place on Earth matches the Moon or Mars in every way, so instead of ranking one “best match,” TerraTwin breaks a lunar south-pole base and a Mars outpost into specific requirements (temperature, terrain, regolith type, aridity, lighting, caves) and scores the entire Earth against each using NASA Earth, Moon, and Mars data. A set-cover optimizer then selects the smallest set of reachable sites that together cover the most requirements for both missions, highlighting sites useful for both. Each site gets a data-backed profile card marking it as a known analog or a newly identified candidate. TerraTwin also reports what cannot be tested anywhere on Earth. Validated against established analogs like Atacama and Haughton Crater, it helps mission planners test equipment efficiently and discover new, under-characterized analog sites.
details:
TerraTwin is an interactive planner that answers: which Earth sites, including ones never used as analogs, should NASA test at before building bases on the Moon and Mars, and what can't be tested on Earth at all?

What it does. No single Earth site matches the Moon or Mars on every factor. So instead of ranking one "best match", TerraTwin breaks a lunar south-pole base and a Jezero-like Mars outpost into 14 testable requirements: extreme cold, polar low-angle light, regolith analogs, impact craters, ground ice, lava tubes, barren surfaces, hyperaridity, UV, low pressure, daily temperature swing, basaltic terrain, ancient lakebeds, and dust and wind. It scores 71 Earth sites from 0 to 1 on each, using NASA POWER climate data and cited geology. A greedy weighted max-coverage solver then picks the smallest portfolio of sites that covers the most requirements, with a penalty for hard-to-reach sites. Everything Earth cannot test (reduced gravity, vacuum and a thin CO₂ atmosphere, 40 K shadowed craters, charged lunar dust, cosmic radiation, the two-week lunar night) is always listed and never scored.

Results. With Moon and Mars together, five sites cover 95% of the weighted testable needs: Harrat Khaybar, Haughton Crater, Ojos del Salado, Allan Hills and Wadi Rum. Four of the five are new candidates. Users can switch between Moon, Mars or both, choose a mission purpose (rover testing, habitat and isolation, ice extraction, astrobiology), edit weights, change the portfolio size and reachability penalty, or show new candidates only. Every site has a card with its raw NASA values, per-requirement scores, Earth-vs-target comparisons and sources.

Benefits and impact. TerraTwin turns analog selection into a transparent, data-backed decision tool. It shows where a small, affordable set of field campaigns gives the most coverage, points to promising new sites (for example Mount Erebus and Mistastin Crater for the Moon, Licancabur and Monturaqui for Mars, and Lonar Crater and Puga Valley in India), and says honestly which risks need other test methods.

Validation and honesty. We tested the method against 16 sites already used as analogs: 12 rank in the top half of all candidates and 7 in the top quarter. That is below our 60% target, and we report it rather than tune it away. The low-ranked analogs were chosen for chemistry or operations, which TerraTwin doesn't score.

Creativity. Portfolio optimization plus an explicit "what Earth can't test" gap list, instead of a single best match. It's presented on an interactive 3D globe with diminishing-returns feedback for every pick.

Tools. Python (data pipeline, NASA POWER API), vanilla JavaScript ES modules (scoring engine and UI), globe.gl / three.js (3D globe), the Node.js test runner, and Vercel (static hosting). It has no backend and no login.

Factors we considered. Data traceability (every number links to a dataset or paper), reachability, Earth-relative thresholds (no Earth value reaches Moon or Mars values), missing data shown rather than hidden, accessibility and phone use, and the honest limits of point sampling and tag-based geology.
